tool.name: TopographyAlongLines
tool.summary: Adds attribute fields describing the topography along each line of a polyline feature class -- length, surface ratio, uphill/downhill and slope statistics, direction statistics, sinuosity, fractal dimension, and more. Elevation comes from the polylines' own Z values or is sampled from a DEM by bilinear interpolation; each line is reduced to straight three-dimensional segments and every statistic is computed from those segments. The fields are written into the input feature class.
tool.usage:
This tool characterizes the terrain a line crosses. For each line it samples elevation along the route, breaks the route into short straight three-dimensional segments, and reduces those segments to a set of attributes: how long the line is on the ground versus in three dimensions, how much of it climbs or descends, how steep it is, which way it heads, how much it meanders, and how convoluted it is. You choose which attributes to compute and which field each one is written to, much like the Calculate Geometry Attributes tool.
Direction of travel. Many of these statistics depend on which way the line goes. A line that climbs 100 m from west to east descends 100 m from east to west; its uphill and downhill lengths swap, and its mean direction flips. Every direction-dependent statistic here (cumulative elevation gain and loss, net elevation change, uphill/downhill length and proportion, and mean direction) describes the line travelling in the direction of its geometry -- from its first vertex to its last. If you need them measured the other way, reverse the line first (e.g. with the Flip or Reverse tools). The direction-independent statistics (lengths, surface ratio, slope spread, sinuosity, fractal dimension, circular/angular variance, and so on) are unaffected by the direction of travel.
Elevation source. If the polylines are Z-enabled you may use their own Z values, in which case each line's existing vertices become the segment breakpoints. Otherwise, or by choice, elevation is sampled from a DEM: sample points are placed along each line at a regular ground interval equal to the smaller of the DEM's cell width and height (plus the first and last vertex of every part), the points are projected into the DEM's own coordinate system -- the DEM itself is never projected, which would degrade it -- and the elevation at each point is found by bilinear interpolation. Elevation units are read from the DEM's (or the feature class's) vertical coordinate system when defined; otherwise you are asked to choose Meters or Feet.
The segment model. Each straight segment has a start and end with X, Y, and Z. Its planimetric length is the geodesic (on-the-spheroid) horizontal distance between its ends; its surface length is the true three-dimensional distance, the hypotenuse of the horizontal length and the elevation change (Pythagoras). On a flat 30 m DEM each interior segment is about 30 m long, and a little longer where the ground rises or falls. Multipart lines are handled part by part: the first and last vertex of every disconnected piece are included, and no segment is ever created across the gap between pieces.
The statistics:
• Lengths: Planimetric Length (geodesic) is the sum of the segments' horizontal lengths; Surface Length (geodesic) is the sum of their three-dimensional lengths; Surface Ratio is surface length divided by planimetric length (1 on flat ground, larger over rough or steep terrain). • Uphill / downhill / flat: Length Uphill, Length Downhill, and Length Perfectly Flat are the summed surface lengths of the climbing, descending, and level segments, and the matching Proportion statistics divide each by the total surface length. • Elevation: Cumulative Elevation Gain and Cumulative Elevation Loss sum the rises and falls; Net Elevation Change is gain minus loss; Total Vertical Relief Traveled is gain plus loss (the total climbing and descending); Minimum Elevation, Maximum Elevation, and Elevation Range describe the sampled elevations; Minimum Elevation X / Y and Maximum Elevation X / Y report the coordinates of the lowest and highest sampled point along the line, in the polyline dataset's coordinate system units (when that extreme elevation occurs at more than one sampled point, the first such point along the line is reported). • Slope: Average Slope is the surface-length-weighted mean of the absolute segment slopes; Slope Standard Deviation and RMS Slope are their weighted spread; Minimum Slope and Maximum Slope are the shallowest and steepest segment slopes. • Direction: Mean Direction is the surface-length-weighted mean heading; Mean Resultant Length measures how tightly the headings cluster (0 to 1); Circular Variance and Circular Standard Deviation (Mardia and Jupp; Fisher) and Angular Variance and Angular Deviation (Batschelet) are alternative measures of directional spread; the Rayleigh p-value tests whether the line has a preferred direction. • Shape and roughness: Total Curvature is the summed absolute turning between consecutive segments; Sinuosity (3D) is the surface length divided by the straight-line three-dimensional distance between the line's ends (per part for multipart lines); Fractal Dimension measures how convoluted the route is in map view (1 for a straight line, toward 2 for a highly tortuous one); Reversal Count is how many times the line switches between climbing and descending.
Units. Lengths are reported in the Length Unit you choose; elevation statistics (gain, loss, net, relief, minimum, maximum, range) are reported in the DEM's or polylines' elevation units; the surface ratio, proportions, sinuosity, circular and angular variance, mean resultant length, and fractal dimension are unitless; the reversal count is an integer count. Slope statistics are always computed internally in degrees so that averages are true; the Average, Minimum, and Maximum slopes are then converted to the Slope Unit you choose (degrees or percent), while the slope standard deviation and RMS slope have no exact conversion and are always reported in degrees. Directions and directional standard deviations are reported in degrees (azimuth, measured clockwise from north). The metadata of every field created states the units it is in.
Choosing fields. In the Surface Attributes list, each row pairs a property (statistic) with the output field it is written to. The Property column comes first: use its drop-down to check off several statistics at once, and each new row's field name is filled in automatically from the property (for example, Surface Length becomes Surface_Length) -- you can edit any of them. The Field column offers a dropdown of the input's existing editable numeric fields, in the order they appear in the feature class; you may instead pick one of those or type your own name. New fields are created for you (as a double-precision field, or a long integer for the reversal count). Turn on "List existing fields by alias" to choose existing fields by their alias instead of their name; if you type a new value in that mode, a properly named field is created with your text set as its alias. Pointing a statistic that can be fractional at an existing integer field is flagged, because the value would be rounded.
Fractal dimension requires a range of scales, so it can only be estimated for lines long enough to span one (roughly six times the sampling interval or more); shorter lines are left null and the tool reports how many. Fractal dimension is a debated measure of path tortuosity (Benhamou 2004) and is meaningful only over the range of scales the sampling supports.
References: Directional statistics follow Mardia, K. V., and P. E. Jupp. 2000. Directional Statistics. Wiley (https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470316979); Fisher, N. I. 1993. Statistical Analysis of Circular Data. Cambridge University Press (https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511564345); and Batschelet, E. 1981. Circular Statistics in Biology. Academic Press (ISBN 0-12-081050-6); the formulas used here are given in Jenness, J. 2012. Directional data. Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Fractal dimension uses the divider method of Mandelbrot, B. B. 1967. How long is the coast of Britain? Statistical self-similarity and fractional dimension. Science 156:636-638 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.156.3775.636), as applied to paths by Nams, V. O. 2005. Using animal movement paths to measure response to spatial scale. Oecologia 143:179-188 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-004-1804-z). Sinuosity, the straightness index, and path tortuosity follow Benhamou, S. 2004. How to reliably estimate the tortuosity of an animal's path. Journal of Theoretical Biology 229:209-220 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2004.03.016) and Batschelet (1981). The surface-length concept follows Jenness, J. S. 2004. Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839.

dialogReference.para: The polyline feature class to add topography attributes to. The fields are written into this dataset. If a selection is active, only the selected features are processed.

Where elevations come from. Z values from the polylines uses the lines' own vertex Z values (available only for Z-enabled feature classes; each existing vertex becomes a segment breakpoint). DEM raster samples elevation from a DEM. When the input is not Z-enabled this is set to DEM automatically.

The DEM to sample elevation from (used when the elevation source is DEM). Sample points are placed along each line at a ground interval equal to the smaller of the cell width and height, projected into the DEM's coordinate system, and interpolated bilinearly. The DEM itself is not projected.

The elevation units (Meters or Feet) of the DEM or of the polylines' Z values. Filled in and locked automatically when the vertical coordinate system defines them; you are asked to choose only when they are undefined.

Each row pairs a Property (the statistic to compute) with the output Field it is written to. Use the Property column's drop-down to check off several statistics at once; each new row's field name is then filled in automatically (you can edit it). The Field column also lists the input's existing editable numeric fields in feature-class order, so you may instead pick an existing field or type your own name (created automatically). See the tool description for the meaning of each property and its units. The Minimum Elevation X / Y and Maximum Elevation X / Y properties report coordinates in the polyline dataset's own coordinate system (even when the elevations were sampled from a DEM in a different coordinate system, the winning point is projected back), and when the extreme elevation occurs at more than one sampled point the first such point along the line is reported.

param.name: use_aliases
param.displayname: List existing fields by alias (instead of name)

dialogReference.para: When on, the field dropdown lists existing fields by their alias rather than their name. Selecting an alias writes to that field; typing a new value creates a properly named field with your text set as its alias.

The unit for all length statistics (planimetric and surface lengths, uphill/downhill/flat lengths): Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles, Yards, or Nautical Miles. Elevation statistics are always reported in the elevation units, not this unit.

The unit for the Average, Minimum, and Maximum slope statistics: Degrees or Percent (rise/run x 100). Slopes are always computed internally in degrees; the standard deviation and RMS of slope have no exact conversion and are always reported in degrees. Used only when a slope statistic is selected.

scriptExample.title: Topography along Lines example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Compute several attributes from a DEM. The Surface Attributes value table is a list of [property, field] pairs (property first). Valid Property strings are exactly: "Planimetric Length (geodesic)", "Surface Length (geodesic)", "Surface Ratio", "Length Uphill", "Proportion Uphill", "Cumulative Elevation Gain", "Length Downhill", "Proportion Downhill", "Cumulative Elevation Loss", "Length Perfectly Flat", "Proportion Perfectly Flat", "Net Elevation Change", "Average Slope", "Slope Standard Deviation", "Minimum Slope", "Maximum Slope", "RMS Slope", "Mean Direction", "Mean Resultant Length", "Circular Variance", "Angular Variance", "Circular Standard Deviation", "Angular Deviation", "Rayleigh p-value", "Total Curvature", "Fractal Dimension", "Sinuosity (3D)", "Minimum Elevation", "Minimum Elevation X", "Minimum Elevation Y", "Maximum Elevation", "Maximum Elevation X", "Maximum Elevation Y", "Elevation Range", "Total Vertical Relief Traveled", "Reversal Count". elev_source: "DEM raster" or "Z values from the polylines". length_unit: "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles", "Yards", "Nautical Miles". slope_unit: "Degrees", "Percent".
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.TopographyAlongLines( in_lines=r"C:\Project\Trails.gdb\trails", elev_source="DEM raster", in_dem=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", elev_units="Meters", surface_attributes=[ ["Surface Length (geodesic)", "SurfLen"], ["Surface Ratio", "SurfRatio"], ["Cumulative Elevation Gain", "ElevGain"], ["Average Slope", "AvgSlope"], ["Sinuosity (3D)", "Sinuosity"]], use_aliases=False, length_unit="Meters", slope_unit="Degrees")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Adds topographic-roughness attribute fields (length, surface ratio, uphill/downhill and slope statistics, direction statistics, sinuosity, fractal dimension, and more) to a polyline feature class by sampling elevation along each line and reducing it to straight 3-D segments; geodesic, correct on geographic data, with per-field units metadata.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Reduces each line of a polyline feature class to straight three-dimensional segments -- sampling elevation from the lines' own Z values or from a DEM by bilinear interpolation at a regular ground interval (sample points projected into the DEM's coordinate system, never the DEM) -- and writes chosen statistics into attribute fields. Planimetric and surface lengths are geodesic; slopes are computed in degrees and optionally reported in percent; directions and directional dispersion follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), and Batschelet (1981); fractal dimension uses the divider method (Mandelbrot 1967; Nams 2005); sinuosity is three-dimensional. Direction-dependent statistics describe the line in the direction of its geometry. Multipart lines are handled per part with no bridging. Every output field's metadata states its units. References: Mardia, K. V., and P. E. Jupp. 2000. Directional Statistics. Wiley. Fisher, N. I. 1993. Statistical Analysis of Circular Data. Cambridge University Press. Batschelet, E. 1981. Circular Statistics in Biology. Academic Press. Mandelbrot, B. B. 1967. Science 156:636-638. Nams, V. O. 2005. Oecologia 143:179-188. Benhamou, S. 2004. Journal of Theoretical Biology 229:209-220. Jenness, J. S. 2004. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839.
